sectionTitle: The Haber process and the use of NPK fertilisers (chemistry only)
topic: The Haber process and the use of NPK fertilisers (chemistry only)

specStatements.text: The Haber process is used to manufacture ammonia, which can be used to produce nitrogen-based fertilisers.
The raw materials for the Haber process are nitrogen and hydrogen.
Students should be able to recall a source for the nitrogen and a source for the hydrogen used in the Haber process.

The purified gases are passed over a catalyst of iron at a high temperature (about 450°C) and a high pressure (about 200 atmospheres). Some of the hydrogen and nitrogen reacts to form ammonia. The reaction is reversible so some of the ammonia produced breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen:
On cooling, the ammonia liquefies and is removed. The remaining hydrogen and nitrogen are recycled.
(HT only) Students should be able to:
interpret graphs of reaction conditions versus rate
apply the principles of dynamic equilibrium in Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium to the Haber process
explain the trade-off between rate of production and position of equilibrium
explain how the commercially used conditions for the Haber process are related to the availability and cost of raw materials and energy supplies, control of equilibrium position and rate.
Compounds of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are used as fertilisers to improve agricultural productivity. NPK fertilisers contain compounds of all three elements.

Industrial production of NPK fertilisers can be achieved using a variety of raw materials in several integrated processes. NPK fertilisers are formulations of various salts containing appropriate percentages of the elements.
Ammonia can be used to manufacture ammonium salts and nitric acid.
Potassium chloride, potassium sulfate and phosphate rock are obtained by mining, but phosphate rock cannot be used directly as a fertiliser.
Phosphate rock is treated with nitric acid or sulfuric acid to produce soluble salts that can be used as fertilisers.
recall the names of the salts produced when phosphate rock is treated with nitric acid, sulfuric acid and phosphoric acid
compare the industrial production of fertilisers with laboratory preparations of the same compounds, given appropriate information.

concepts.definition: The industrial process that manufactures ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen. The purified gases are passed over an iron catalyst at about 450 degrees C and about 200 atmospheres.
The compound NH3 made by the Haber process. It is the starting point for nitrogen-based fertilisers, and is not itself spread on fields as the finished fertiliser.
A substance fed into an industrial process. For the Haber process the raw materials are the two reactant gases, nitrogen and hydrogen.
The nitrogen for the Haber process comes from the air, which is about 78% nitrogen.
The hydrogen for the Haber process is obtained from natural gas (methane) or other hydrocarbons.
The catalyst used in the Haber process. It speeds up the rate at which equilibrium is reached but does not change the position of equilibrium, so it does not change the yield.

A reaction in which the products can react to re-form the reactants. In the Haber process some of the ammonia formed breaks down again into nitrogen and hydrogen, so the reaction never goes to completion.

concepts.term: Word equation for the Haber process
concepts.definition: The specification states the reaction as: nitrogen +hydrogen ⇌ ammonia. The double arrow shows that the reaction is reversible.
On cooling, the ammonia condenses to a liquid at a much higher temperature than nitrogen or hydrogen do, so it can be run off and removed while the other two gases stay as gases.
The nitrogen and hydrogen that have not reacted are passed back into the reactor instead of being wasted, which raises the overall conversion and cuts costs.
How quickly ammonia is produced. Raising the temperature, raising the pressure and adding the iron catalyst all increase the rate.
The state reached in a closed system when the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so the amounts of nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia stay constant although both reactions continue.

How far the equilibrium lies towards the products. Raising the pressure moves it towards ammonia because there are fewer gas molecules on the ammonia side; raising the temperature moves it away from ammonia because the forward reaction is exothermic.
The proportion of the nitrogen and hydrogen that is converted into ammonia at equilibrium. A high yield and a high rate need opposite temperatures, which is why a compromise is needed.

The conditions actually used in industry: about 450 degrees C gives a lower yield than a cool reactor would but a workable rate, and about 200 atmospheres gives a lower yield than very high pressure would but avoids the cost and danger of stronger plant.
A fertiliser containing compounds of all three of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, the elements with symbols N, P and K.
A mixture made in fixed proportions so that it does a job. An NPK fertiliser is a formulation of several salts blended to give appropriate percentages of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
A salt made by reacting ammonia with an acid, for example ammonium nitrate from ammonia and nitric acid, or ammonium sulfate from ammonia and sulfuric acid.
An acid manufactured from ammonia. It is used both to make ammonium nitrate and to treat phosphate rock.
A mined rock containing insoluble phosphate compounds. It supplies phosphorus but cannot be used directly as a fertiliser.
Potassium chloride, potassium sulfate and phosphate rock are dug out of the ground rather than synthesised. The potassium salts can be used in fertilisers without further reaction.
A fertiliser has to dissolve in water in the soil before a plant root can take it up, which is why insoluble phosphate rock is first converted into soluble salts.
The mixture of calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate made by treating phosphate rock with sulfuric acid.
The calcium phosphate made by treating phosphate rock with phosphoric acid.

A laboratory preparation is a batch: one small quantity is made, filtered and crystallised by hand. Industrial fertiliser production runs continuously on a large scale through several integrated processes.

misconceptions.question: What does the Haber process actually produce?
misconceptions.correct: The Haber process produces ammonia. The ammonia is reacted further before it becomes a fertiliser.
misconceptions.misconception: The nitrogen and hydrogen are obtained by breaking ammonia or ammonium compounds back down into their elements.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The process is always introduced as 'how we feed the world', so students collapse the two steps into one.
misconceptions.correction: Ammonia is the product. Reacting it with nitric acid gives ammonium nitrate, and that is the fertiliser.

misconceptions.question: Where does each raw material gas come from?
misconceptions.correct: Nitrogen comes from the air; hydrogen comes from natural gas (methane) or other hydrocarbons.
misconceptions.misconception: Both gases are separated out of the air.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember 'nitrogen from the air' and assume the second gas must arrive the same way, and air does contain traces of hydrogen compounds as water vapour.
misconceptions.correction: Air is about 78% nitrogen but almost no hydrogen. The hydrogen is obtained from natural gas.

misconceptions.question: Is the hydrogen for the Haber process made by electrolysis of water?
misconceptions.correct: The usual industrial source is natural gas (methane), because it is much cheaper than electrolysis.
misconceptions.misconception: The hydrogen is made by electrolysing water, since water is free.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Electrolysis of water is the hydrogen source students meet first in class, so it is the one they recall.
misconceptions.correction: Electrolysis needs large amounts of electricity. Industry reacts methane from natural gas to obtain hydrogen.

misconceptions.question: Why is a temperature of about 450 degrees C used?
misconceptions.correct: 450 degrees C is a compromise: a hotter reactor is faster but gives a lower yield of ammonia.
misconceptions.misconception: 450 degrees C is used because it gives the greatest possible yield of ammonia.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students assume the chosen condition must be the best one for yield, because that is what the plant is trying to maximise.
misconceptions.correction: The forward reaction is exothermic, so yield falls as temperature rises. 450 degrees C buys rate at the cost of yield.

misconceptions.question: What does the iron catalyst do to the amount of ammonia made at equilibrium?
misconceptions.correct: Nothing. It speeds up the rate at which equilibrium is reached, leaving the position of equilibrium unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: The iron catalyst increases the yield of ammonia.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Catalyst' is filed under 'makes the reaction better', and more ammonia per hour is confused with more ammonia at equilibrium.
misconceptions.correction: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium arrives sooner but at the same position.

misconceptions.question: What does it mean that the Haber reaction is reversible?
misconceptions.correct: Some of the ammonia formed breaks down again into nitrogen and hydrogen, so not all the reactants are converted.
misconceptions.misconception: The reaction runs forwards until the reactants are used up, then runs backwards.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The double arrow is read as 'first one way, then the other' rather than as both happening together.
misconceptions.correction: Both directions happen at the same time in the reactor, which is why the ammonia has to be removed as it forms.

misconceptions.question: Which arrow belongs in the Haber process equation?
misconceptions.correct: A double arrow, because the reaction is reversible.
misconceptions.misconception: A single arrow, because ammonia is the product.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Nearly every equation students have written before uses a single arrow, so it is the default.
misconceptions.correction: The specification writes nitrogen +hydrogen ⇌ ammonia. The double arrow is part of the chemistry.

misconceptions.question: Is the product of the Haber process ammonia or ammonium?
misconceptions.correct: Ammonia, NH3. Ammonium, NH4+, is the ion found in ammonium salts.
misconceptions.misconception: The Haber process makes ammonium.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two words differ by two letters and both appear in this topic, so they are easily swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Ammonia is the neutral molecule made in the reactor. Ammonium ions only appear once ammonia reacts with an acid.

misconceptions.question: How is the symbol equation for the Haber process balanced?
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students balance the hydrogen but forget that two ammonia molecules are needed to use both nitrogen atoms.
misconceptions.correction: Two nitrogen atoms enter, so two NH3 molecules must leave. Check both elements before stopping.

misconceptions.question: Which substance liquefies when the mixture leaving the reactor is cooled?
misconceptions.correct: The ammonia liquefies; the nitrogen and hydrogen stay as gases and are recycled.
misconceptions.misconception: The nitrogen and hydrogen liquefy and the ammonia is left as a gas.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know air can be liquefied to separate nitrogen, and transfer that to this reactor.
misconceptions.correction: Ammonia condenses at about -33 degrees C, far higher than nitrogen or hydrogen, so it is the one that turns liquid first.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the nitrogen and hydrogen that did not react?
misconceptions.correct: They are recycled back into the reactor.
misconceptions.misconception: They are burnt off or released, because the reaction has finished with them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In laboratory work leftover reactants are simply discarded, so students carry that habit over to industry.
misconceptions.correction: Recycling the unreacted gases raises the overall conversion and avoids wasting expensive raw materials.

misconceptions.question: What does a graph of rate against temperature for the Haber process show?
misconceptions.correct: Rate rises as temperature rises, at every pressure.
misconceptions.misconception: Rate falls as temperature rises, because the yield falls.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that yield falls with temperature and then read the rate axis as if it were a yield axis.
misconceptions.correction: Yield and rate respond to temperature in opposite ways. Check the axis label before describing the trend.

misconceptions.question: What does a graph of yield against pressure show?
misconceptions.correct: Yield rises as pressure rises, because there are fewer gas molecules on the ammonia side.
misconceptions.misconception: Yield falls as pressure rises, because the gases are squashed together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Squashing' is imagined as making the reaction harder rather than as favouring the side with fewer molecules.
misconceptions.correction: Four molecules of gas become two, so higher pressure shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia.

misconceptions.question: What is happening at dynamic equilibrium?
misconceptions.correct: Both reactions are still going, at equal rates, so the amounts stay constant.
misconceptions.misconception: Both reactions have stopped.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Nothing appears to change, and 'no change' is read as 'nothing is happening'.
misconceptions.correction: Equilibrium is dynamic: the forward and reverse reactions continue but cancel each other out.

misconceptions.question: At equilibrium, how do the amounts of reactants and products compare?
misconceptions.correct: They are constant, but not necessarily equal to one another.
misconceptions.misconception: There are equal amounts of nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Equilibrium' suggests 'balance', and balance is pictured as equal quantities on each side.
misconceptions.correction: Equal rates, not equal amounts. The position of equilibrium decides how much of each is present.

misconceptions.question: What is the effect of removing the ammonia as it liquefies?
misconceptions.correct: The equilibrium shifts towards ammonia, so more nitrogen and hydrogen react.
misconceptions.misconception: It has no effect on the equilibrium, it just collects the product.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think of removal as happening after the chemistry, rather than as a change the system responds to.
misconceptions.correction: Taking a product out moves the equilibrium to replace it, which is why removal and recycling raise the overall conversion.

misconceptions.question: Why not run the Haber process at a much lower temperature?
misconceptions.correct: The yield would be higher but the reaction would be far too slow to be commercially useful.
misconceptions.misconception: A low temperature is used, because it gives the highest yield.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The exothermic argument is learned in isolation and applied without asking how long the plant would have to wait.
misconceptions.correction: A high yield reached too slowly is worth nothing. The temperature chosen trades yield for rate.

misconceptions.question: What does the trade-off between rate and equilibrium position mean?
misconceptions.correct: The conditions chosen are not the best for either rate or yield on their own, but give the most ammonia per day at acceptable cost.
misconceptions.misconception: The conditions chosen are simply the ones that give the fastest reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rate is the more familiar idea, so the equilibrium half of the argument gets dropped.
misconceptions.correction: Both matter. A very hot reactor is fast but converts little; the compromise maximises production overall.

misconceptions.question: Why is a pressure of only about 200 atmospheres used?
misconceptions.correct: Higher pressures would raise the yield but need much stronger plant, more energy to compress the gases, and carry greater risk.
misconceptions.misconception: 200 atmospheres is used because it gives the highest possible yield.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students assume industry always picks the condition that maximises yield, ignoring the cost of the pipework.
misconceptions.correction: Yield keeps rising with pressure, so the limit is economic and about safety, not chemical.

misconceptions.question: Why is the nitrogen taken from the air?
misconceptions.correct: Air is free and about 78% nitrogen, so it is the cheapest available source.
misconceptions.misconception: Air is used because nitrogen from the air is more reactive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for a chemical reason when the reason is availability and cost.
misconceptions.correction: The specification links the conditions and raw materials to availability and cost. Air costs nothing to obtain.

misconceptions.question: Is the iron catalyst used up during the Haber process?
misconceptions.correct: No. The catalyst is not used up, which is part of why it is economic.
misconceptions.misconception: The iron catalyst only works within fixed limits: it stops working below 450 degrees C and is destroyed above 200 atmospheres.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Anything added to a reaction is assumed to be a reactant.
misconceptions.correction: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up, so one charge of iron lasts a long time.

misconceptions.question: Which elements do the letters in NPK stand for?
misconceptions.correct: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
misconceptions.misconception: Nitrogen, phosphorus and krypton, because K is the symbol for krypton.
misconceptions.whyItArises: K looks like it should belong to a word beginning with K, and potassium does not.
misconceptions.correction: K is the symbol for potassium, from its Latin name kalium. Krypton is Kr.

misconceptions.question: Is an NPK fertiliser a single compound?
misconceptions.correct: No, it is a formulation: several salts blended to give appropriate percentages of the three elements.
misconceptions.misconception: NPK is one compound containing nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The single label NPK suggests a single substance with a single formula.
misconceptions.correction: No one salt supplies all three elements economically, so NPK fertilisers are mixtures made to a recipe.

misconceptions.question: What can ammonia be used to manufacture?
misconceptions.correct: Ammonium salts and nitric acid.
misconceptions.misconception: Ammonia is used to manufacture sulfuric acid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sulfuric acid appears in the same fertiliser topic, so it gets attached to ammonia as well.
misconceptions.correction: Sulfuric acid is made from sulfur, not from ammonia. Ammonia gives ammonium salts and nitric acid.

misconceptions.question: Can phosphate rock be spread on fields as it is?
misconceptions.correct: No. Its phosphate compounds are insoluble, so it must first be treated with an acid.
misconceptions.misconception: Phosphate rock is mined and spread straight onto fields as a phosphorus fertiliser.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Because the rock is mined ready-made, students see no reason for a further step.
misconceptions.correction: Plants take up dissolved ions, so the phosphate must be converted into soluble salts before it is any use.

misconceptions.question: How are potassium chloride and potassium sulfate obtained?
misconceptions.correct: They are obtained by mining, and can be used in fertilisers without further reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: They are manufactured from potassium metal in a chemical plant.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect every named salt in an industrial topic to be a manufactured product.
misconceptions.correction: Potassium chloride and potassium sulfate are mined, like phosphate rock. Unlike it, they are already suitable for use.

misconceptions.question: What is made when phosphate rock is treated with sulfuric acid?
misconceptions.correct: Single superphosphate, a mixture of calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate.
misconceptions.misconception: Only calcium sulfate is made.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students track the sulfuric acid and forget that the phosphate has to end up somewhere as well.
misconceptions.correction: Both salts are present. The product is described as single superphosphate.

misconceptions.question: What is made when phosphate rock is treated with nitric acid?
misconceptions.correct: Phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate.
misconceptions.misconception: Ammonium nitrate is made.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ammonium nitrate is the fertiliser students know best, so it is offered whenever nitric acid appears.
misconceptions.correction: There is no ammonia in this step. Nitric acid on phosphate rock gives phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate.

misconceptions.question: What is triple superphosphate?
misconceptions.correct: Calcium phosphate, made by treating phosphate rock with phosphoric acid.
misconceptions.misconception: It is a mixture of calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two superphosphates are learned as a pair and their compositions get swapped.
misconceptions.correction: The sulfate only appears when sulfuric acid is used. Phosphoric acid leaves calcium phosphate alone.

misconceptions.question: How does industrial fertiliser production differ from a laboratory preparation?
misconceptions.correct: Industry runs continuously on a huge scale through several integrated processes; the laboratory makes a single small batch by hand.
misconceptions.misconception: The two are essentially the same, just with bigger apparatus in the factory.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The same salt is made in both, so students assume the method must also be the same.
misconceptions.correction: Scale changes the method: continuous operation, recycled reactants and integrated plants have no laboratory equivalent.

misconceptions.question: How is an ammonium salt made from ammonia?
misconceptions.correct: Ammonia is reacted with an acid, for example nitric acid to give ammonium nitrate.
misconceptions.misconception: Ammonia is reacted with an alkali.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ammonia solution is alkaline, so students mistakenly pair it with another alkali rather than with an acid.
misconceptions.correction: Ammonia behaves as a base here. Base plus acid gives a salt, so ammonia plus nitric acid gives ammonium nitrate.

misconceptions.question: Why must a fertiliser salt be soluble?
misconceptions.correct: Plant roots can only take up ions that are dissolved in the water in the soil.
misconceptions.misconception: A fertiliser should be insoluble so that rain does not wash it away.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason about run-off, which is a real problem, and conclude that insolubility must be desirable.
misconceptions.correction: Solubility is essential for uptake. Run-off is a separate drawback of soluble fertilisers, not a reason to use insoluble ones.

mcqs.stem: What is manufactured directly by the Haber process?

options.text: Ammonia, which is then used to make nitrogen fertilisers
options.rationale: The Haber process manufactures ammonia, and that ammonia is used to produce nitrogen-based fertilisers.

options.text: Ammonium nitrate, ready for spreading onto farm fields
options.rationale: Joins 'Haber process' straight to 'fertiliser' and misses the reaction with an acid in between.

options.text: Nitrogen and hydrogen, made by breaking down ammonia
options.rationale: Nitric acid is made from ammonia later on, so its name is attached to the same industrial story.

options.text: Nitrogen and hydrogen, drawn straight from the air
options.rationale: Confuses what goes into the reactor with what comes out, and has both gases coming from the air.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of gases are the raw materials for the Haber process?

options.text: Nitrogen and oxygen gas
options.rationale: The two main gases in air, offered because students remember that air is one of the sources.

options.text: Nitrogen and hydrogen
options.rationale: The specification states that the raw materials for the Haber process are nitrogen and hydrogen.

options.text: Hydrogen and water
options.rationale: Wrong: water is not a raw material; hydrogen is extracted from methane, nitrogen from air.

options.text: Hydrogen and oxygen
options.rationale: The elements in water, chosen by students who think of hydrogen only as something split from water.

mcqs.stem: A student is asked to give a source of the nitrogen used in the Haber process. Which answer is correct?

options.text: It is obtained from the air, together with the hydrogen
options.rationale: Wrong: only nitrogen comes from air; hydrogen comes from methane, not the air.

options.text: It is obtained by heating ammonium salts in large vessels
options.rationale: Ammonium salts are a product of this industry rather than a feedstock for it.

options.text: It is obtained from the air, which is about 78% nitrogen
options.rationale: Air is the source of the nitrogen and is about 78% nitrogen by volume.

options.text: It is obtained by electrolysis of concentrated brine
options.rationale: Electrolysis of brine gives chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide, not nitrogen.

mcqs.stem: Which is the usual industrial source of the hydrogen used in the Haber process?

options.text: Electrolysis of water, which splits it into elements
options.rationale: Electrolysis does give hydrogen, but the electricity needed makes it far too costly at this scale.

options.text: The air, as hydrogen is one of the gases present in it
options.rationale: Air holds almost no free hydrogen; only the nitrogen is taken from the air.

options.text: Heating ammonia so that it splits into its elements
options.rationale: This reverses the reaction the plant is trying to run, so it cannot be the source.

options.text: Natural gas, which consists mainly of methane
options.rationale: Hydrogen is obtained from natural gas (methane) or from other hydrocarbons.

mcqs.stem: Which conditions are used in the Haber process?

options.text: An iron catalyst, 450 degrees C and 20 atmospheres
options.rationale: The temperature is right but the pressure is ten times too low.

options.text: An iron catalyst, 450 degrees C and 200 atmospheres
options.rationale: The specification gives an iron catalyst, a high temperature of about 450 degrees C and a high pressure of about 200 atmospheres.

options.text: A nickel catalyst, 450 degrees C and 200 atmospheres
options.rationale: Nickel is the catalyst used to add hydrogen to alkenes, and gets borrowed for this process too.

options.text: An iron catalyst, 45 degrees C and 20 atmospheres
options.rationale: A cool reactor would give a better yield, which is why this tempts, but the rate would be far too slow.

mcqs.stem: What is the effect of the iron catalyst in the Haber process?

options.text: It increases the yield of ammonia formed at equilibrium
options.rationale: A catalyst does not move the position of equilibrium, so the yield is unchanged.

options.text: It only speeds up the reaction at 450 degrees C or above
options.rationale: Catalysts are not used up; the same charge of iron serves for a long time.

options.text: It speeds up the rate at which the equilibrium is reached
options.rationale: The catalyst raises the rate of the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium arrives sooner.

options.text: It stops the ammonia formed from breaking down again
options.rationale: The reverse reaction still happens; the catalyst speeds that up as well.

mcqs.stem: The Haber reaction is reversible. What does this mean inside the reactor?

options.text: All the nitrogen and hydrogen react, then some ammonia breaks down
options.rationale: Treats the two directions as happening one after the other rather than together.

options.text: The reaction runs forwards during the day and backwards at night
options.rationale: A literal reading of 'reversible' as a switch between two separate phases.

options.text: The ammonia formed can never break down once it is made
options.rationale: Describes an irreversible reaction, which is what a single arrow would mean.

options.text: Some of the ammonia breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen
options.rationale: The specification states that the reaction is reversible, so some of the ammonia produced breaks down again.

mcqs.stem: Which equation for the Haber process is written as the specification gives it?

options.text: nitrogen +hydrogen ⇌ammonia
options.rationale: This is the word equation exactly as the specification states it, with the double arrow for a reversible reaction.

options.text: ammonia ⇌nitrogen + hydrogen
options.rationale: Writes the reverse reaction as though it were the process being carried out.

options.text: nitrogen + hydrogen → ammonia
options.rationale: A single arrow would mean the reaction goes to completion, which it does not.

options.text: nitrogen + hydrogen ⇌ ammonium
options.rationale: Ammonium is the ion in ammonium salts; the product here is ammonia.

mcqs.stem: Which balanced symbol equation represents the Haber process?

options.text: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ NH3
options.rationale: The hydrogen balances but only one nitrogen atom is accounted for on the right.
Wrong: the Haber process is reversible and must use the ⇌ sign, not a single arrow.
Two nitrogen atoms and six hydrogen atoms appear on each side, so the equation is balanced.

options.text: N2 + H2 ⇌ NH3
options.rationale: Neither element balances; the coefficients have simply been left out.

mcqs.stem: The mixture leaving the reactor is cooled. What happens?

options.text: The nitrogen and the hydrogen liquefy and are then drawn off
options.rationale: Both of these gases condense far below the temperature at which ammonia does.

options.text: All three gases liquefy together and are then distilled
options.rationale: Cooling is used precisely because the three do not condense at the same temperature.

options.text: The ammonia decomposes back to nitrogen and hydrogen
options.rationale: Cooling favours the forward reaction, and the ammonia is being separated, not destroyed.

options.text: The ammonia liquefies and is removed from the gas mixture
options.rationale: On cooling, the ammonia liquefies and is removed, leaving the other two gases behind.

mcqs.stem: What happens to the nitrogen and hydrogen that have not reacted?

options.text: They are recycled back through the reactor
options.rationale: The remaining hydrogen and nitrogen are recycled, so the raw materials are not wasted.

options.text: They are burnt to provide heat for the reactor
options.rationale: Sounds economical but destroys valuable purified gases.

options.text: They are released into the air as harmless gases
options.rationale: Treats leftover reactants as waste, as they often are in laboratory work.

options.text: They are cooled and sold as by-products
options.rationale: Plausible-sounding but pointless, since they were bought as feedstock for this plant.

mcqs.stem: A graph shows the rate of the Haber reaction against temperature at a fixed pressure. What does it show?

options.text: The rate falls steadily as the temperature is increased
options.rationale: Confuses the rate axis with a yield axis; yield is what falls as temperature rises.

options.text: The rate rises as the temperature is increased
options.rationale: Higher temperature means more frequent and more energetic collisions, so the rate increases.

options.text: The rate falls as the temperature rises because the yield falls
options.rationale: Wrong: higher temperature raises collision frequency, so the rate rises, not falls.

options.text: The rate is highest at the lowest temperatures on the graph
options.rationale: Wrong: rate increases with temperature; the lowest temperatures give the slowest rate.

mcqs.stem: A graph shows the percentage yield of ammonia against pressure at 450 degrees C. What is the trend, and why?

options.text: Yield falls, because squashing the gases hinders the reaction
options.rationale: Pressure is treated as an obstacle rather than as favouring the side with fewer molecules.

options.text: Yield is constant, because pressure only changes the rate
options.rationale: Pressure does change the rate, but it also moves the position of this equilibrium.

options.text: Yield falls, because ammonia is squeezed back into its elements
options.rationale: Reverses the true shift; higher pressure favours the ammonia side, not the reactant side.

options.text: Yield rises, because there are fewer gas molecules in the ammonia
options.rationale: Four molecules of gas become two, so raising the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia.

mcqs.stem: Inside a sealed Haber reactor at equilibrium, what is true?

options.text: Both reactions are still going on at the same rate
options.rationale: At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates, so amounts stay constant.

options.text: Both the forward and reverse reactions have stopped
options.rationale: Reads 'no observable change' as 'nothing is happening'.

options.text: The amounts of all three gases are now equal
options.rationale: Confuses equal rates with equal quantities.

options.text: Only the forward reaction is taking place
options.rationale: If only one direction ran, the amounts would keep on changing.

mcqs.stem: Ammonia is removed from the mixture as it liquefies. What is the effect on the equilibrium?

options.text: There is no effect, since the ammonia has already been made
options.rationale: Treats separation as something that happens after the chemistry is finished.

options.text: It shifts towards the ammonia side, so more gas reacts
options.rationale: Removing a product moves the equilibrium to replace it, raising the overall conversion.

options.text: It shifts back towards the nitrogen and hydrogen instead
options.rationale: Gets the direction the wrong way round; the system replaces what is taken away.

options.text: It stops the reverse reaction from happening at all
options.rationale: The reverse reaction still runs; only its rate falls as ammonia is removed.

mcqs.stem: Why is the Haber process not run at a much lower temperature than 450 degrees C?

options.text: Because the yield of ammonia would be lower at low temperatures
options.rationale: Reverses the equilibrium argument; a cooler reactor would actually give a higher yield.

options.text: Because the iron catalyst does not work at all below 450 C
options.rationale: Invents a threshold; the catalyst still works, but everything happens far too slowly.

options.text: Because the reaction would then be far too slow to use
options.rationale: A low temperature gives a better yield but so slow a rate that the plant would be uneconomic.

options.text: Because a lower temperature would shift the equilibrium back
options.rationale: The exothermic forward reaction is favoured by cooling, not disfavoured.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the trade-off between rate of production and position of equilibrium?

options.text: The conditions give the most ammonia per day, not the best yield or the fastest rate
options.rationale: A compromise temperature accepts a lower equilibrium yield in exchange for a workable rate of production.

options.text: The conditions chosen are simply those that give the fastest possible reaction
options.rationale: Drops the equilibrium half of the argument, keeping only the more familiar idea of rate.

options.text: The conditions chosen are the ones giving the highest possible yield of ammonia
options.rationale: Drops the rate half of the argument; a very high yield reached slowly is worthless.

options.text: The catalyst is chosen so that the yield and the rate can both be maximised
options.rationale: A catalyst changes rate only, so it cannot remove the conflict.

mcqs.stem: Why is a pressure of about 200 atmospheres used rather than a far higher one?

options.text: Because a higher pressure would reduce the yield of the ammonia made
options.rationale: Yield keeps rising with pressure, so this is not the reason for the limit.

options.text: Because the iron catalyst is destroyed above 200 atmospheres
options.rationale: Invents a chemical limit where the real limit is cost and safety.

options.text: Because stronger plant, more energy and greater risk cost more
options.rationale: Yield would rise further, but the extra pipework, compression energy and hazard are not worth the gain.

options.text: Because 200 atmospheres gives the greatest possible yield
options.rationale: Assumes the chosen condition must be the optimum for yield.

mcqs.stem: The nitrogen for the Haber process is taken from the air. Which reason best explains this choice?

options.text: Nitrogen taken from the air is more reactive than nitrogen from a tank
options.rationale: Looks for a chemical explanation where the reason is economic.

options.text: Air is free and is about 78% nitrogen, so it is the cheapest source
options.rationale: Commercial conditions and raw materials are chosen for availability and cost, and air costs nothing.

options.text: Air already contains all the hydrogen that is needed for the reaction
options.rationale: Air holds almost no hydrogen; the hydrogen comes from natural gas.

options.text: Nitrogen from the air needs no purification before it is used
options.rationale: The gases are purified before entering the reactor, so this is not the reason.

mcqs.stem: An NPK fertiliser contains compounds of which three elements?

options.text: Nitrogen, phosphorus and krypton, symbol K
options.rationale: K does not stand for krypton, and krypton is an unreactive gas of no use to a plant.

options.text: Nitrogen, potassium and carbon, from K
options.rationale: Both the element chosen and the reasoning behind the letter are wrong here.

options.text: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium salts
options.rationale: Names a class of compound in place of the element potassium.

options.text: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium
options.rationale: NPK fertilisers contain compounds of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

mcqs.stem: Why is an NPK fertiliser described as a formulation?

options.text: Because it is one single compound whose formula contains all three elements
options.rationale: A formulation is a mixture, not a single compound with one formula.

options.text: Because it uses only insoluble salts so the rain cannot wash it away
options.rationale: Wrong: a formulation is a blend of soluble salts mixed to set N, P and K percentages.

options.text: Because it is a mixture of salts blended to give set percentages of N, P and K
options.rationale: NPK fertilisers are formulations of various salts containing appropriate percentages of the elements.

options.text: Because it is made in one reactor from a single mined raw material
options.rationale: Industrial production uses a variety of raw materials in several integrated processes.

mcqs.stem: Ammonia from the Haber process can be used to manufacture which substances?

options.text: Ammonium salts and nitric acid
options.rationale: The specification states that ammonia can be used to manufacture ammonium salts and nitric acid.

options.text: Ammonium salts and sulfuric acid
options.rationale: Half right, but sulfuric acid is made from sulfur, not from ammonia.

options.text: Nitric acid and sulfuric acid
options.rationale: Both acids appear in this topic, so both get attached to ammonia.

options.text: Nitric acid and a compound called NPK
options.rationale: Phosphates come from mined phosphate rock, not from ammonia.

mcqs.stem: Which of these fertiliser raw materials are obtained by mining?

options.text: Phosphate rock and ammonium nitrate, but not the potassium salts
options.rationale: Wrong: potassium chloride and potassium sulfate are mined; ammonium nitrate is manufactured.

options.text: Nitric acid and phosphate rock, but not the potassium salts
options.rationale: Wrong: potassium salts are mined; nitric acid is manufactured, not mined.

options.text: Only phosphate rock, since the potassium salts are made in plants
options.rationale: Both of the potassium salts named in the specification are mined as well.

options.text: Potassium chloride, potassium sulfate and phosphate rock
options.rationale: The specification lists these three as obtained by mining.

mcqs.stem: Why can phosphate rock not be used directly as a fertiliser?

options.text: Because the rock must be dried out before it is spread
options.rationale: Wrong: phosphate rock cannot be used directly because its compounds do not dissolve.

options.text: Because the phosphate compounds in it do not dissolve
options.rationale: Plant roots take up dissolved ions, so the insoluble phosphate must first be made into soluble salts.

options.text: Because the rock must first be ground into a much finer powder
options.rationale: Wrong: the real barrier is that the phosphate compounds are insoluble, not particle size.

options.text: Because it dissolves so readily that the rain washes it away
options.rationale: Reverses the actual problem, which is that it does not dissolve at all.

mcqs.stem: Phosphate rock is treated with sulfuric acid. What is produced?

options.text: Calcium sulfate only, with the phosphate left in the rock
options.rationale: Follows the sulfuric acid and forgets that the phosphate must end up somewhere too.

options.text: Calcium phosphate only, known as triple superphosphate
options.rationale: That is the product of treating the rock with phosphoric acid, not with sulfuric acid.

options.text: Ammonium sulfate, which supplies nitrogen and sulfur
options.rationale: Brings in ammonium although no ammonia is used in this step.

options.text: Single superphosphate: calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate
options.rationale: Treating phosphate rock with sulfuric acid gives single superphosphate, a mixture of the two salts.

mcqs.stem: Phosphate rock is treated with nitric acid. Which products are formed?

options.text: Ammonium nitrate and calcium oxide
options.rationale: Ammonium nitrate needs ammonia, which is not used in this reaction.

options.text: Phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate
options.rationale: Treating phosphate rock with nitric acid produces phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate.

options.text: Calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate
options.rationale: That is single superphosphate, which is made using sulfuric acid instead.

options.text: Calcium nitrate and calcium oxide
options.rationale: Half right on the calcium nitrate, but the phosphate is simply dropped.

mcqs.stem: Which salt is produced when phosphate rock is treated with phosphoric acid?

options.text: Calcium phosphate, called triple superphosphate
options.rationale: Phosphoric acid converts phosphate rock into calcium phosphate, known as triple superphosphate.

options.text: Calcium sulfate, the salt in single superphosphate
options.rationale: Single superphosphate is a mixture and it comes from sulfuric acid.

options.text: Calcium phosphate mixed with some calcium sulfate
options.rationale: The sulfate only appears when sulfuric acid is used.

options.text: Ammonium phosphate, made from the rock alone
options.rationale: Ammonium phosphate needs ammonia as well as phosphoric acid.

mcqs.stem: A student makes ammonium sulfate in the laboratory by titration and crystallisation. How does industrial production of the same salt differ?

options.text: It reacts the ammonia with an alkali rather than an acid
options.rationale: Wrong: both routes use ammonia and sulfuric acid; industry differs by running continuously at scale.

options.text: It is carried out in exactly the same way, but with larger apparatus
options.rationale: Scale changes the method, not just the size of the glassware.

options.text: It runs continuously on a large scale, with reactants recycled
options.rationale: Industrial production is continuous, large scale and integrated, whereas the laboratory prepares a single small batch.

options.text: It adds phosphorus and potassium to make the compound NPK
options.rationale: Industrial fertilisers are formulations of salts, so a single pure salt is not the aim.

mcqs.stem: In a Haber reactor at 200 atmospheres the rate of production is 9, 21 and 33 tonnes per hour at 350, 450 and 550 degrees C. The percentage yield at the same three temperatures is 55, 28 and 12. What do the data show?

options.text: The rate is highest at 350 degrees C, where the yield is highest
options.rationale: Swaps the two sets of figures over. It is the yield that falls from 55 to 12.

options.text: The rate rises with temperature while the yield falls
options.rationale: The rate figures rise from 9 to 33 while the yield figures fall from 55 to 12.

options.text: Both the rate and the yield fall at higher temperatures
options.rationale: Reads the rate column as though it were a yield column, so both are said to fall.

options.text: The rate and the yield are both highest at 450 degrees C
options.rationale: Assumes the temperature industry chose must be the best one for both. Neither peaks there.

mcqs.stem: At 450 degrees C the rate of ammonia production is 12 tonnes per hour at 100 atmospheres, 24 at 200 atmospheres and 45 at 400 atmospheres. What do these data show?

options.text: The rate falls as the gases are squashed up
options.rationale: Applies the idea that squashing hinders the reaction instead of reading the figures.

options.text: The rate stops rising beyond 200 atmospheres
options.rationale: The last step, 24 to 45 tonnes per hour, is still nearly a doubling, so the rise has not levelled off.

options.text: Raising the pressure does not change the rate
options.rationale: The figures almost quadruple from 100 to 400 atmospheres, so pressure clearly changes the rate.

options.text: Doubling the pressure roughly doubles the rate
options.rationale: 12 to 24 and 24 to 45: each doubling of the pressure roughly doubles the rate of production.
